Case_Content:
Man, 71 years old, metastatic right colon cancer (KRAS mutated). After 8 cycles FOLFOX: progression of two lesions segment VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Progression on chemotherapy, no surgical window at this stage.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning:  
- Liver lesions are limited to two lesions (segments VII and VIII) with a maximum diameter of 5.2 cm, suggesting a technically feasible hepatic resection (right hepatectomy or extended right hepatectomy).  
- However, critical information required to confirm surgical feasibility is missing:  
  • Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio compatibility with surgery (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery – Missing).  
  • Presence of vascular contact or invasion (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion – Missing) and detailed arterial anatomy (ArterialAnatomy – Missing).  
  • Status of the primary colorectal tumor (Has the colorectal primary tumor been already resected? – Missing) and any obstructive or bleeding symptoms (Missing).  
- Because these missing data directly impact whether a safe, curative resection can be performed, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending clarification of these points.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Systemic therapy adjustment – Switch to a second‑line regimen (e.g., FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) given progression on FOLFOX and KRAS‑mutated status (no anti‑EGFR benefit).  
2. Restaging after 2–3 cycles – Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to:  
   • Define lesion borders, vascular involvement, and biliary anatomy.  
   • Re‑assess FLR volume (CT volumetry or MRI).  
3. Evaluation of the primary tumor – Perform colonoscopy and cross‑sectional imaging of the right colon to determine resectability, presence of obstruction, perforation, or bleeding. If resectable and symptomatic, plan right hemicolectomy.  
4. Multidisciplinary decision –  
   • If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % in a cirrhotic liver) and no major vascular invasion, proceed to curative surgery.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) to hypertrophy the future remnant, then re‑image to confirm adequacy.  
5. Surgical sequencing –  
   • Preferred simultaneous resection (right hemicolectomy + right hepatectomy) in a fit 71‑year‑old if operative risk acceptable and FLR adequate.  
   • If operative risk high or FLR marginal, adopt a staged approach: first resect the colon primary, allow recovery, then perform liver resection (or PVE‑induced hypertrophy) after systemic disease control.  
6. Post‑operative systemic therapy – Resume or continue second‑line chemotherapy (FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) for at least 3–6 months post‑resection, with serial CEA monitoring (baseline 950 ng/mL) and imaging every 3 months.  
7. Clinical trial consideration – Evaluate eligibility for trials targeting KRAS‑mutated metastatic colorectal cancer (e.g., KRAS‑G12C inhibitors, immunotherapy combinations) given aggressive disease biology.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- FLR ratio compatibility with surgery (FutureLiverRemnantFLRRatio).  
- Presence and extent of vascular contact/invasion and detailed arterial anatomy (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion, ArterialAnatomy).  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected or not) and any obstructive/bleeding symptoms (ColorectalPrimaryTumorPostResectionCharacterization, PresenceOfSymptomsForObstruction/Perforation/Bleeding).  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (GradeOfDifferentation).  
- Results of liver MRI (Has liver MRI been performed?).  
- Assessment for brain metastasis (ExtrahepaticBrainInvolvement).  

These items are essential to finalize resectability judgment and to design a safe, curative surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient shows progression of liver disease under FOLFOX with enlargement of two lesions in segments VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) and markedly elevated CEA (950 ng/mL). This radiologic progression under systemic therapy indicates biologically aggressive disease and makes a complete R0 resection with adequate oncologic control not achievable at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Given progression on FOLFOX, a change of systemic regimen is required according to MDT decision (e.g., switch to FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is to regain disease control and potentially create a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains progressive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• Consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of all liver lesions on MRI.
B. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
E. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
F. Previous systemic treatments received and tolerance.
G. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case a surgical window appears.
H. Evolution of CEA after first-line chemotherapy.
I. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
1. Completeness: The two recommendations differ significantly in their approach to resectability and management. Recommendation 1 considers the case potentially resectable pending further information, focusing on a resectability approach with systemic therapy adjustment, imaging, and potential surgical intervention. Recommendation 2, however, deems the case currently unresectable due to biological aggressiveness and suggests systemic therapy with close monitoring for a potential future surgical opportunity. Therefore, they do not cover the same clinical domains or management components.

2. Step-by-step concordance: In step 1, the assessments of resectability differ: Recommendation 1 states the case is potentially resectable, while Recommendation 2 considers it unresectable at this stage. In step 2, the management plans diverge, with Recommendation 1 planning for possible surgery after systemic therapy and imaging, and Recommendation 2 focusing on systemic control with potential future reconsideration for surgery if major response occurs.

3. Case-tailoring concordance: The recommendations do not align in terms of case-specific details. Recommendation 1 includes specific surgical planning, FLR assessments, and potential local surgical interventions depending on several factors. Recommendation 2 focuses more on systemic therapy adaptation and future potential surgical assessment, emphasizing a different strategy due to perceived aggressiveness.

4. Missing data concordance: The recommendations identify different missing data points important for their respective strategies. Recommendation 1 requires data to confirm resectability (e.g., FLR ratio, vascular involvement details), while Recommendation 2 prioritizes understanding of systemic disease status and future potential resectability conditions (e.g., MRI distribution, MSS/MSI status). Thus, they do not agree on the critical missing information.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient now has three residual liver lesions each <2 cm after a major response to chemotherapy, which is compatible with a curative‑intent liver resection. However, decisive information required to confirm feasibility is missing: (a) whether the rectal primary has already been resected or requires neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, (b) precise hepatic segmental location of the residual lesions and any vascular or biliary involvement, (c) the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, and (d) confirmation that there are no extra‑hepatic metastases on thoraco‑abdominal imaging. Because these specific prerequisites are absent, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the missing assessments.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Obtain complete staging: perform contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone or brain metastases that were not reported.  
• Clarify status of the rectal primary: if not yet resected, assess tumor stage (MRI pelvis) and decide on neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (long‑course RT ± capecitabine) followed by total mesorectal excision; if already resected, confirm R0 status.  
• Review liver MRI in detail (or obtain high‑resolution liver protocol CT) to map the three residual lesions to hepatic segments, evaluate proximity to major vessels or bile ducts, and calculate FLR volume.  
• If FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % in steatotic liver) and no major vascular/biliary invasion, proceed with a parenchymal‑sparing liver resection (non‑anatomic wedge resections or segmentectomy) aiming for negative margins (R0).  
• If FLR is insufficient, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy to augment FLR before definitive resection.  
• Schedule liver surgery either simultaneous with rectal resection (if both procedures are limited and patient fitness permits) or staged (rectal resection first, then liver resection after recovery), based on multidisciplinary consensus and patient comorbidities.  
• After surgical clearance, resume adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for a total of 6 months, considering addition of anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type status, especially if postoperative CEA remains elevated.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Primary tumor resection status and need for neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy.  
• Detailed hepatic segment involvement, vascular/biliary contact, and arterial anatomy.  
• Quantitative FLR ratio (volumetric assessment).  
• Results of thoraco‑abdominal imaging to exclude extra‑hepatic disease.  
• Grade of differentiation of the rectal carcinoma (affects prognosis and adjuvant decisions).  
These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI and precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
D. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Status and treatment plan of the rectal primary tumor : Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
G. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
**Completeness:** Both recommendations cover resectability assessment, preoperative staging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative therapy. They extensively discuss the need for imaging to confirm the state of metastases, the FLR calculation, the management of the rectal primary, and the importance of postoperative systemic therapy. Therefore, they are complete in scope. 

**Step Concordance:** The recommendations differ in their assessment of resectability. Recommendation 1 labels the patient as 'potentially resectable' pending further assessments, while Recommendation 2 considers the patient 'resectable' but requires detailed reassessment. Additionally, the management plans diverge as Recommendation 1 proposes a stepwise systemic therapy and surgery sequence based on FLR, whereas Recommendation 2 emphasizes a strategy involving the resection or ablation of all original metastatic sites and integrates rectal management concurrently. 

**Case Tailoring Concordance:** The two recommendations diverge in their approaches to case-specific clinical details. Recommendation 1 focuses on specific metrics like FLR percentage and the status of the rectal primary, considering factors like RAS wild-type status for potential anti-EGFR therapy. Recommendation 2, however, includes elements such as minimally invasive surgical techniques, the PRODIGE 23 protocol for rectal management, and the use of ERAS protocols, which are not mentioned in Recommendation 1. 

**Missing Data Concordance:** The critical missing data identified in the two recommendations differ significantly. Recommendation 1 points out the need for detailed hepatic segment involvement, vascular/biliary contact, and future liver remnant ratio. Recommendation 2, while overlapping in FLR estimation, emphasizes localization of disappeared metastases, MSS/MSI mutation status, and specific rectal tumor details on MRI that are not mentioned in Recommendation 1.

Case_Content:
Woman, 67 years old, T4N2M1 transverse colon cancer, multiple bilobar liver metastases, CEA 600 ng/mL. On FOLFOX: overall stability, two new lesions detected at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Limited progression on treatment, question of changing protocol.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the current data do not allow a definitive judgment of hepatic resectability because key anatomic variables are missing (NumberOfMetastases, MaximumLesionDiameter, HepaticSegmentsInvolved, PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion, FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery). In addition, the status of the primary colorectal tumor (Has the colorectal primary tumor been already resected?) is unknown, and the molecular phenotype (RAS/BRAF/MSI) that would influence peri‑operative systemic therapy is absent. These missing pieces are decisive for planning a curative‑intent operation; therefore resection can only be considered after they are obtained and after an appropriate systemic‑therapy response is achieved.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Obtain complete staging:  
  • Perform a liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define number, size, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement and to calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio.  
  • Re‑evaluate the primary tumor with contrast‑enhanced CT/MRI of the abdomen and pelvis; determine whether it is resectable or symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding, perforation).  
  • Obtain tissue for molecular profiling (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H) from the primary tumor or a metastatic site.  
- Optimize systemic therapy:  
  • Because limited progression is observed on FOLFOX, switch to a second‑line regimen (e.g., FOLFIRI) combined with a targeted agent selected according to the molecular results (anti‑EGFR if RAS wild‑type, anti‑VEGF if RAS‑mutated or unknown).  
  • Consider adding a biologic agent (bevacizumab or cetuximab) and continue treatment for 2–3 months to achieve maximal tumor shrinkage.  
- Address the primary lesion:  
  • If the primary tumor remains in situ and is symptomatic, perform resection (or a diverting colostomy) before or concurrently with liver surgery. If asymptomatic, it may be resected in a staged fashion after liver disease is controlled.  
- Re‑assess resectability after systemic therapy:  
  • Repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT and liver MRI; evaluate response of hepatic lesions and calculate FLR.  
  • If lesions are reduced to a limited number (generally ≤4) with adequate FLR (>30 % in a normal liver, >40 % after chemotherapy), plan curative liver resection—either simultaneous with primary resection if feasible, or staged (primary first, then liver).  
  • If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) before definitive resection.  
- Post‑operative management:  
  • Continue systemic therapy (maintenance or adjuvant) based on response and molecular profile.  
  • Monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Molecular phenotype of the colorectal primary (RAS, BRAF, MSI status).  
- Detailed hepatic metastasis characterization (exact number, size, segmental involvement, vascular/biliary contact, and FLR calculation).  
- Status of the primary tumor resection (already resected or still in place, presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms).  
- Results of a liver‑specific MRI (currently missing).  
These items are essential to determine whether a curative‑intent liver resection is feasible and to select the optimal systemic‑therapy regimen.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has multiple bilobar liver metastases with the appearance of two new lesions while on FOLFOX, indicating disease progression under systemic therapy. The tumor burden, bilobar distribution, and ongoing progression make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• The appearance of new lesions under FOLFOX indicates resistance to the current regimen.
• A change of systemic protocol is required according to MDT decision (e.g., switch to FOLFIRI ± targeted therapy depending on molecular profile).
• The objective is to regain disease control and potentially create a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains progressive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• Consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of all liver lesions on MRI.
B. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
E. Patient’s performance status and tolerance for further systemic therapy.
F. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
G. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case a surgical window appears
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
The two recommendations differ substantially across all criteria:

1. **Completeness**: Recommendation 1 considers the case potentially resectable following further assessment and systemic therapy response, covering preoperative staging, systemic therapy optimization, surgical planning, and postoperative management. It outlines a comprehensive plan for obtaining additional diagnostic information and reassessing surgical options. Recommendation 2, conversely, deems the case unresectable due to progression, emphasizing adaptation of systemic therapy and surveillance, offering a different scope and focus than Recommendation 1.

2. **Step Concordance**: The assessments of resectability differ (potentially resectable vs. unresectable). The management strategies are also discordant, with Recommendation 1 aiming for potential resection after systemic therapy, while Recommendation 2 focuses on systemic control and palliative approaches, only reconsidering surgery under markedly improved conditions.

3. **Case Tailoring**: Recommendation 1 details specific molecular and surgical considerations tied to the resectability of both primary and metastatic disease, whereas Recommendation 2 emphasizes systemic therapy resistance and adaptation, noting extrahepatic disease presence and patient's performance status, thus diverging in their tailored approach to the patient's circumstances.

4. **Missing Data Concordance**: Both recommendations highlight important missing data, but Recommendation 2 includes broader considerations such as extrahepatic disease presence, patient's performance status, and liquid biopsies, which are not addressed in Recommendation 1. This results in a mismatch in identified critical data needed to advance management.

Overall, the recommendations are distinct in both their initial assessment and subsequent management approaches, reflecting a lack of alignment across all evaluated criteria.

Case_Content:
Man, 71 years old, history of segment VII resection. Liver MRI: local recurrence at resection site (2.5 cm) and additional nodule segment V. No other lesion at the thoraco CT scan CEA 410 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Localized recurrence on resection scar, complex technical feasibility.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has two liver metastases (segment VII recurrence 2.5 cm and a new nodule in segment V) with no extra‑hepatic disease on thoraco‑CT. However, critical information that directly determines surgical feasibility is missing: future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, extent of vascular contact/invasion, arterial anatomy, and baseline liver function. Without these data we cannot confirm that a safe, curative resection can be performed now; therefore the case is classified as potentially resectable pending further evaluation and/or pre‑operative optimization.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Obtain missing pre‑operative data:  
  – Perform contrast‑enhanced CT volumetry (or MRI) to calculate FLR ratio and assess liver parenchyma quality.  
  – Review contrast‑enhanced imaging (or repeat MRI/CT) to define vascular relationships of both lesions (portal/hepatic veins, hepatic artery).  
  – Obtain liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance if available) and assess performance status.  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) as neoadjuvant treatment to:  
  – Evaluate tumor biology (response of CEA, radiologic shrinkage).  
  – Potentially downsize lesions if vascular involvement is borderline.  
• Re‑image after 2–3 cycles of chemotherapy: repeat MRI and CT volumetry.  
  – If FLR is <30 % (or <40 % in a steatotic liver), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left lobe before resection.  
• Once adequate FLR and clear vascular anatomy are confirmed, proceed to repeat hepatic resection:  
  – Parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomy of the recurrent lesion in segment VII and segmentectomy or wedge resection of the segment V nodule, using intra‑operative ultrasound to achieve R0 margins.  
  – Ensure preservation of sufficient functional liver tissue.  
• Post‑operative management:  
  – Resume/adapt systemic therapy based on pathological response and molecular profile (once obtained).  
  – Monitor CEA serially; consider adjuvant chemotherapy if high‑risk features are present.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
The most crucial missing items that must be obtained to finalize the plan are:  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio compatibility with surgery.  
• Presence and extent of vascular contact or invasion (portal/hepatic veins, hepatic artery).  
• Detailed arterial anatomy and any variant anatomy.  
• Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance).  
• Status of prior systemic therapy (has chemotherapy already been given?).  
• Molecular phenotype and grade of the primary colorectal tumor (to guide systemic regimen).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a 2.5 cm local recurrence at the prior segment VII resection site and an additional nodule in segment V, without reported extrahepatic disease. This represents localized intrahepatic recurrence in a previously operated posterior segment. Despite the scar location and technical complexity, both lesions appear amenable to local treatment while preserving adequate inflow/outflow and functional reserve. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of prior liver resection, this pattern is considered potentially resectable, pending detailed vascular and volumetric assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative vascular and anatomical assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define the relationship of the segment VII recurrence to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and scar tissue.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (current liver) and assess inflow/outflow preservation.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and multifocal recurrence, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Consider peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA (410 ng/mL) and recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) is advisable to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.

B. Combined local treatment strategy
• Given the scar location and technical difficulty, a combined approach is appropriate:
– Either Parenchymal-sparing resection or thermo-ablation of the segment V lesion.
– Resection of the segment VII scar recurrence depending on its relationship to vascular structures and the extent of adhesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both approaches.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles if administered.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII recurrence on MRI.
B. Exact volumetric assessment of the remaining liver (future liver remnant).
C. Patient’s current liver function and performance status.
D. Details of previous chemotherapy received before/after the prior liver surgery.
E. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full staging.
F. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
G. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular status of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Details of timing between previous resection and current recurrence
I. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
Completeness: Both recommendations cover the major clinical domains such as resectability assessment, preoperative staging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative therapy and surveillance. They both address the need for preoperative imaging to assess vascular relationships, FLR calculations, the use of systemic chemotherapy, and postoperative management.

Step-by-step concordance: Both recommendations agree that the lesions are potentially resectable pending further evaluation. They both propose a similar management sequence involving preoperative imaging, systemic chemotherapy, and surgical intervention. The key steps of imaging, chemotherapy, and surgery are aligned in both recommendations.

Case-tailoring concordance: Both recommendations reflect considerations specific to the case, such as molecular profile (e.g., MSS/MSI), lesion-specific surgical approaches, and factors like CEA levels and technical complexity due to prior surgery. They both incorporate these elements into their plans.

Missing data concordance: While there is significant overlap in identified missing information, such as FLR, vascular relationships, and liver function, Recommendation 2 provides additional details, such as liquid biopsies and the need for confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full staging. Therefore, there is partial but not complete alignment in missing data emphasis.

Case_Content:
Woman, 54 years old, mid-rectal T3N1 tumor with five bilobar liver metastases and a right lung metastasis at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 330 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Limited hepato-pulmonary involvement, evaluation of a possible combined approach.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The case cannot be declared resectable upfront because decisive information is lacking. Specifically, the size, segmental distribution and vascular/biliary involvement of the five bilobar liver lesions, the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, and the resectability of the right‑lung metastasis are not provided. Moreover, the primary rectal tumor has not yet been addressed (resection status, need for neoadjuvant radiotherapy). These missing data require neoadjuvant systemic therapy and further imaging before a definitive surgical plan can be made.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for RAS‑wild‑type, synchronous metastatic disease (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab or FOLFOX + cetuximab).  
• After 2–3 months, restage with high‑resolution liver MRI, PET‑CT, and repeat chest CT to:  
    – Determine response of liver lesions, exact size, segmental involvement, and any vascular/biliary contact.  
    – Calculate FLR ratio and decide if portal vein embolization or staged hepatectomy is needed.  
    – Assess the right‑lung nodule for size, location relative to vessels/bronchi and resectability.  
• If imaging shows that all liver lesions can be cleared with an adequate FLR (≥20 % in a normal liver, ≥30 % after chemotherapy), plan a combined or staged surgical approach:  
    – Primary rectal cancer: proceed with total mesorectal excision; if the tumor remains T3 with threatened margin, give neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy before resection.  
    – Liver: perform parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy of all five lesions; if FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization first or a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS.  
    – Lung: if the solitary right‑lung metastasis is technically resectable, schedule pulmonary metastasectomy (segmentectomy or wedge) either synchronously with liver surgery (if patient fitness permits) or in a staged fashion after hepatic resection. If not surgically resectable, consider stereotactic body radiotherapy.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant therapy: continue systemic treatment (e.g., maintenance bevacizumab or anti‑EGFR) and monitor CEA and imaging every 3–6 months.

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Exact size, segmental location and vascular/biliary involvement of each liver metastasis.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and ratio to total liver.  
- Resectability assessment of the right‑lung metastasis (size, lobar distribution, relation to bronchi/vessels).  
- Status of the primary rectal tumor (has it been resected? need for neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy?).  
- Histologic grade of differentiation of the primary tumor.  
- Confirmation of systemic therapy already given (if any) and response assessment.  
- PET‑CT results to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  

These pieces of information are required to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases and a single right lung metastasis in the setting of a mid-rectal T3N1 tumor, without other reported sites. Limited, potentially resectable extrahepatic disease (lung) does not contraindicate a curative-intent strategy if all sites can be completely treated. Classification: Potentially resectable

Because these data are required to determine whether an adequate future liver remnant can be achieved and whether down‑staging can render the portal pedicle invasion resectable, the case cannot be labeled “Resectable upfront.” At the same time, there is no absolute contraindication (no extra‑hepatic disease reported), so the disease is not “Not resectable.” Hence the appropriate category is “Potentially resectable,” contingent on specific prerequisite actions and missing information.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated, high‑volume disease (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months, aiming for tumor and liver‑metastasis down‑staging.  
• During the same period, schedule a right‑sided colectomy (standard oncologic right hemicolectomy) either before or after the initial chemotherapy cycles, depending on the patient’s clinical status and multidisciplinary consensus.  
• After neoadjuvant chemotherapy, repeat high‑resolution liver MRI and CT to:  
    – Re‑assess number, size, and segmental distribution of liver lesions.  
    – Re‑evaluate the extent of portal pedicle invasion and arterial anatomy.  
    – Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) volume and FLR ratio.  
• If FLR is insufficient for an anatomic right (or extended right) hepatectomy, perform right portal vein embolization (PVE) to induce hypertrophy of the left liver lobe.  
• Re‑image 4–6 weeks after PVE to confirm adequate FLR (generally ≥ 25 % in a normal liver, ≥ 30–40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected).  
• When FLR is adequate and portal pedicle invasion has responded or can be resected safely, proceed with staged liver surgery:  
    – First stage: right hepatectomy (or extended right hepatectomy) with en‑bloc removal of involved portal structures if feasible, using vascular reconstruction as needed.  
    – Second stage (if required): completion of left‑lobe resection or ablation of residual lesions after recovery.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy (continuation of the same regimen or switch to maintenance) for at least 6 months, guided by pathological response and postoperative CEA trend.  
• Throughout, monitor CEA levels and perform surveillance imaging every 3 months for the first 2 years.

• Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric assessment.  
• Exact hepatic segmental involvement and maximum/minimum lesion diameters to plan the extent of resection.  
• Status of the primary colon tumor (whether it has already been resected).  
• Details of arterial anatomy and presence of portal vein thrombosis that could affect vascular reconstruction.  
• Confirmation of whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered.  
• Brain imaging results (to exclude occult cerebral metastasis).
